bib.title: Non-stationary Bandits (Chapter 31, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: book chapter, Bandit Algorithms (Cambridge University Press); year inferred from the book, not printed in the chapter text

question: How should regret be defined and minimised when the environment changes over time, in adversarial and stochastic finite-armed bandits?
contributions: Define non-stationary (tracking) regret with m-1 change points by enlarging the competitor class (Sec 31.1)
Exp4 bound and a matching lower bound Omega(sqrt(nmk)) (Sec 31.1)
Efficient policy: online stochastic mirror descent on a clipped simplex (Theorem 31.1)
Negative result: no stochastic policy can match the omniscient log-regret rate with abrupt changes (Theorem 31.2)
Notes on discounted UCB, sliding-window UCB, drift and total-variation models

results.claim: Exp3 (plain negentropy mirror descent) does not work for non-stationary bandits: R_n2 >= c n (exercise 31.3).

results.claim: Clipping the simplex to A = P_{k-1} intersect [alpha,1]^k keeps the policy from committing too hard to one arm, so change points can still be discovered.
results.setup: Online stochastic mirror descent, unnormalised negentropy potential, alpha in [0,1/k]
results.quote:
The clipping ensures the algorithm does not commit too
hard to any single arm.

results.claim: Under bounded total variation V_n=sum ||mu_t - mu_{t+1}||_inf <= V, a policy gets R_n <= C (V k log k)^{1/3} n^{2/3}, nearly minimax tight, and it can adapt without knowing V.

results.quote: Rn ≤C(V k log(k))1/3n2/3

results.claim: With reflected-Brownian-motion drift of arm means, regret is necessarily linear because the best arm changes with constant probability each round.

limits: Chapter gives no experiments; only exercise 31.4 asks the reader to compare Exp3, Exp3-IX and the mirror-descent variant on k=2, n=1000.
Algorithms for stochastic switching (discounted/sliding-window UCB) are stated without regret theorems here; analysis is deferred to Garivier and Moulines 2011.
No change-point detection algorithm (CUSUM, GLR style) is described; the chapter says the discounting/window approach instead and cites multi-scale exploration methods without steps.
Adversarial setting with unknown number of switches and optimal sqrt(mkn log n) regret is open per the authors.
Rewards assumed Gaussian with unit variance in the stochastic section.
practices: Enlarge the comparator class to action sequences with at most m-1 changes when judging a learner in a changing environment (Sec 31.1).
Do not use plain Exp3 on non-stationary problems; clip the simplex to [alpha,1]^k so every arm keeps probability at least alpha (Sec 31.1).
Set alpha=sqrt(m/(nk)) and eta=sqrt(2m log(1/alpha)/(nk)) if m is known; else alpha=sqrt(1/nk), eta=sqrt(log(1/alpha)/nk) at an O(sqrt m) cost (p.381).
Check whether adding context (time of year) removes the apparent non-stationarity before using a non-stationary algorithm (Note 1).
In stochastic settings with abrupt changes use discounting or a sliding window; expect a tuning problem for gamma and tau (Note 2).
Expect to keep exploring suboptimal arms forever if abrupt changes are possible (p.382).

code.snippet: P_{t+1} = argmin_{p in A} eta<p, Yhat_t> + D_F(p, P_t), Yhat_ti = I{A_t=i} y_ti / P_ti; two steps: Ptilde_{t+1,i} = P_ti exp(-eta Yhat_ti), then P_{t+1} = argmin_{p in A} D_F(p, Ptilde_{t+1}) (projection onto clipped simplex, Exercise 26.12)
